title: Darkhotel
summary: Darkhotel, also reported as DUBNIUM and Zigzag Hail, is an espionage cluster that public reporting has tracked since at least 2007 and that became well known through a 2014 vendor report on attacks against travelling executives. The distinguishing feature is the setting: the operators were reported to have knowledge of, or access to, hotel and conference networks, and they used that position to deliver fake software updates and phishing pages to selected guests. Victims were typically senior people in technology, defence, energy and pharmaceutical companies, chosen while they travelled and were therefore away from the protection of the corporate network. Later reporting described the group using previously unknown flaws in widely installed browser and document plugins, so that a single visit to a prepared page was enough. Evidence is usually found after the traveller returns: an update with an unexpected signer, an implant in a startup location, or outbound connections from the laptop to hosts that other machines in the company never contact. Attribution remains uncertain; reporting has noted language artefacts that suggest a region, but no sponsor has been established publicly.

beginner.definition: Darkhotel is the name for a group that spied on business travellers. Security researchers wrote about it in 2014. The group used hotel and conference networks to reach its targets. It offered fake software updates that installed harmful programs, and the people behind it have never been publicly identified.
beginner.whyItMatters: Executives travel with laptops that hold plans and passwords. Hotel networks are shared with strangers and are hard to trust. This group showed that a traveller can be attacked far from the office. Without advice about travel and updates, a single hotel stay can leak years of work.
howItWorks: The attackers watch who is staying at a hotel, often from inside the hotel network.
They wait until the guest tries to download a common software update.
Instead of the real file, the guest receives a harmful version with the same name.
The harmful file installs a spying program and then removes the obvious traces.
The program quietly reports documents and passwords back to the attackers over the internet.
Later campaigns used flaws in browser plugins, so simply visiting a page was enough.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel lobby where a stranger hands out free phone chargers. They work perfectly, so nobody complains, and guests take them without asking the front desk. One model, given only to a few chosen guests, copies every message from the phone. The hotel staff never see anything wrong at all, and the guests leave the next morning believing the stay was normal. The harm only appears weeks later, on a network far away from the hotel.
takeaways: Treat hotel and airport networks as untrusted, and use your own connection.
Download updates only from the official site or your company's own service.
A clean looking software update can still carry harmful code.

objectives: Explain how a hostile network can deliver a fake software update.
Describe why business travellers are attractive targets for espionage.
Explain how a single browser plugin flaw can lead to a full compromise.
Identify the artefacts left by an implant delivered through a fake update.
Discuss how to describe uncertain attribution in a threat report.
